Jonesville sits in Union County, a genuine mill village built almost entirely around the textile plant that once employed most of its working age population. And when that plant finally closed for good, Jonesville simply stopped changing rather than trying to reinvent itself. The old mill houses, small identical woodframe homes built by the company itself, still line the streets in neat rows exactly as they did when workers rented them from the mill for a few dollars a week. Because unlike Union itself, Jonesville never had much of a downtown commercial district to fall back on. Just the mill, the houses, and the people who worked there. A longtime resident told me her grandfather worked the same mill floor her father later worked. But as of this filming, most of Jonesville's original mill footprint sits exactly as it has for decades, waiting on an investment that hasn't yet arrived. Number 12, St. Matthews. Calhoun County was actually the last county created in South Carolina. [music] The wildcard fact is that LA was once a serious agricultural shipping point. Tobacco and cotton moving through its depot by the train load. And the old warehouses that used to store those crops still stand a block off Main Street, mostly empty now. Sturdy brick buildings waiting for a use nobody's quite found for them yet. LA was actually founded by a single family, the Lattas, who donated the land for the rail depot in the 1880s specifically to attract a stop on the line running between Florence and the North Carolina border. A bet that paid off for decades before the trucking industry gradually pulled freight traffic away from smalltown rail depots across the entire PD. With local preservation groups working to maintain the building, even without an active rail tenant to help fund its upkeep, the town's annual LATA Depot celebrates that same rail history every year with a genuine steam engine display and vendors set up along Main Street. The way traveling salesmen once set up shop the moment a train pulled in. A tradition locals say has barely changed in format since [music] the depot was still handling real freight. Number 10, Saluda. Saluda is the seat of one of South Carolina's smallest counties. Tucked into the ridge region between Colombia and Augusta, an area historically famous [music] for its peach orchards. The town square here is genuinely tiny. a handful of blocks radiating out from a modest courthouse, and it has resisted the kind of chain store sprawl that swallowed the edges of larger county seats nearby. Saluda's population has hovered right around 3,000 people for decades, neither growing nor shrinking dramatically. And locals will tell you that stability is exactly the point. A town that decided somewhere along the way that it didn't need to become anything other than what it already was. [music] The Ridge Spring Moneta area just outside town still produces a meaningful share of South Carolina's peach crop. [music] According to SLEED's own annual figures, a statistic locals bring up with genuine pride, tying it directly to the same close-knit, unchanged character that's kept the town from growing much larger than it already is. The town hosts an annual Saluda Old Home Days festival that pulls former residents back from across the country every year specifically to walk the same square they grew up on. A homecoming tradition that speaks to how many people who leave Saluda for work or college still consider it unmistakably home. Number nine, Due West. Due West is one of the smallest towns in South Carolina. Built entirely around Erskin College, a small liberal arts school founded in 1839 that remains one of the oldest colleges in the state. The Erskin College due west historic district covers nearly 200 acres of 19th and early 20th century buildings. Classical revival architecture that has been carefully preserved rather than renovated into something unrecognizable. Due West has no stoplight, no chain restaurants, and a population that swells and shrinks with the academic calendar. Students filling the tiny downtown during the school year and the whole town going quiet the moment summer break begins. The wildcard fact is that due west got its unusual name from its literal position. Early travelers used the settlement as a landmark because it sat due west of a well-known regional crossroads, a name that stuck for two centuries in counting. Erskin College itself was the first 4-year college in South Carolina to grant degrees to women back in the 1890s, decades ahead of most of its peer institutions in the region. A progressive streak that locals say still shapes the town's quiet, studious character today. With an enrollment of well under a thousand students, Erskin keeps Due West's entire economy and social calendar tied directly to the academic year in a way few other South Carolina towns experience so completely. The modern town small commercial district sits just off Main Street, a handful of familyrun businesses that have served the same few thousand residents for decades, and the local hardware store still operates out of a building that's held the same trade since before most of the current owner's grandparents were born. Number seven, Wall Hala. Walhalla sits at the base of the Blue Ridge Foothills in Aone County, and its downtown has retained a distinctly European feel that no other South Carolina courthouse town quite matches. narrow storefronts, a walkable central square, and a genuine sense that the original German settlers vision for the place mostly stuck. The wildcard fact is that Wall Hollow was once seriously considered as the end point for the Blue Ridge Railroad before the Civil War stopped construction on the Stumphouse Tunnel just a few miles away. A railroad that would have connected Wallala to the Ohio Valley and turned this quiet foothill town into a major transportation hub. A future that never arrived and left Walhalla exactly the small unhurried town it was always meant to stay. A genuine unbroken thread connecting modern Wallala to the 1850s community that founded it.
